recent_posts.title: The Curious Case of the Shallow Session SPAs
recent_posts.summary: Real-world data from multiple sources reveals that Single-Page Applications (SPAs) average only one soft navigation per hard page load, suggesting users don't generate long sessions. This challenges the fundamental trade-off SPAs offer: accepting higher upfront JavaScript costs for faster subsequent interactions. If sessions are truly this shallow, SPA architectures may represent an industry-wide mistake outside specific use cases like document editing or chat. The web performance community needs to investigate whether this data accurately reflects reality, understand what interactions are being measured, and use these insights to steer teams toward more appropriate architectures based on actual session depth rather than FOMO-driven technology choices.

recent_posts.title: From Theory to Tiny: Implementing Compression Dictionaries
recent_posts.summary: Compression Dictionary Transport is a new IETF standard that can reduce file sizes by 60-90% compared to Brotli/GZIP, now supported in Chrome and Edge. Implementation requires architectural decisions around dictionary generation (resource upgrades, standalone dictionaries, or similar resources), CDN configuration, and compression handling. The author details practical challenges including CDN limitations, library compatibility issues, cache keying strategies, and debugging complexities. Despite the implementation overhead, the 4x compression improvement enables benefits like inlining full CSS and aggressive prefetching. With only 13 websites currently using it, early adopters can gain significant performance advantages for 75%+ of web users.

recent_posts.title: Teaching Agents about Performance insights
recent_posts.summary: Building a performance-specialized AI agent requires teaching LLMs to interpret complex telemetry data from Chrome DevTools trace files. The journey involves segmenting trace data into focused problem spaces, using specialized sub-agents with narrow objectives to overcome context window limitations, and implementing workflow-based architectures inspired by Mixture of Experts. The Model Context Protocol enables orchestrating agents to delegate performance analysis to DevTools' internal agents, creating automated workflows for profiling and course correction. Success depends on careful context engineering, keeping sessions focused, and maintaining human verification of AI-generated insights.

recent_posts.title: Seven Chrome DevTools features for debugging and performance analysis
recent_posts.summary: Chrome DevTools offers powerful features beyond basic debugging. The Accessibility Tree reveals what screen readers actually see, Lighthouse User Flows measure performance during real interactions, and network request blocking tests resilience. The Performance panel helps diagnose Core Web Vitals issues like LCP, INP, and CLS while teaching browser behavior. Additional features include dimming third-party code for clearer profiles, the Recorder for capturing reproducible user flows, and remote debugging on Android devices to test real-world performance constraints.

recent_posts.title: Open Source RUM with BasicRUM
recent_posts.summary: BasicRUM is an open source Real User Monitoring tool scheduled for public release in Q1 2026. The self-hosted solution offers GDPR-friendly data ownership, AI-powered chart summaries and chatbot queries, and dashboards for analyzing Core Web Vitals and network metrics. Built with React, TypeScript, and Node.js, it has been battle-tested handling 40 million events over two days on a budget VM. The tool includes dark mode UI, performance bottleneck identification features, and has been validated by three test groups with requirements up to 300K requests per day.

recent_posts.title: Third Parties and Single Points of Failure
recent_posts.summary: Third-party content creates single points of failure (SPOFs) when loaded as render-blocking resources. Analysis of 15.78 million websites shows 67.7% load at least one render-blocking third party, with 60% using different CDNs than their primary content. Common culprits include Google Fonts, CDN-hosted libraries (cdnjs, jsdelivr), and consent management services. The article demonstrates how to detect render-blocking third parties using WebPageTest, Chrome DevTools, and other tools, then test for SPOFs by simulating failures through DNS overrides or request throttling. Self-hosting critical assets and using async loading patterns can eliminate these risks.

recent_posts.title: Tips for making the Performance Panel less overwhelming
recent_posts.summary: Chrome DevTools Performance Panel can be overwhelming for newcomers analyzing page load and interaction traces. Five practical tips make it more approachable: dim third-party code to focus on first-party issues, use search to find specific functions or files, add annotations to document findings and share context, leverage the Insights Panel for automatic detection of common performance problems and Core Web Vitals analysis, and create custom tracks using console.time() or the Performance Measure API to highlight specific function calls. These techniques help identify performance bottlenecks, explain issues to others, and streamline debugging workflows.

recent_posts.title: Chrome DevTools for Debugging Web Performance
recent_posts.summary: A hands-on walkthrough of using Chrome DevTools to identify and debug web performance issues. Covers analyzing Core Web Vitals (LCP, CLS, INP), inspecting network requests, detecting render-blocking resources, examining layout shifts, profiling interactions, and validating optimization hypotheses. Includes practical techniques like environment configuration based on field data, using the Performance panel and Insights sidebar, analyzing CSS media queries, leveraging content-visibility, and optimizing heavy resources like images and videos. Demonstrates real-world analysis of an e-commerce site with specific findings like oversized images, inefficient caching, and heavy JavaScript bundles.

recent_posts.title: Revisiting HTML streaming for modern web performance
recent_posts.summary: HTML streaming allows servers to send HTML progressively rather than in one chunk, enabling browsers to render content as it arrives. HTMS is an experimental project that extends basic streaming with progressive placeholders that can be updated asynchronously within a single HTTP response. This approach delivers early First Contentful Paint, maintains SEO-friendly complete HTML documents, and achieves strong Lighthouse scores without client-side hydration. The technique works best combined with SSR, SSG, or tools like HTMX, though it introduces constraints around error handling once streaming begins and requires careful layout planning.

recent_posts.title: Chasing BFCache navigations
recent_posts.summary: BFCache (Back/Forward Cache) is a browser mechanism that instantly restores pages when users navigate back or forward, preserving the entire page state in memory without reloading. This results in near-zero TTFB, instant FCP/LCP, and zero CLS for 10-20% of navigations. However, BFCache eligibility is fragile and can be broken by Cache-Control: no-store headers, unload events, poorly handled APIs, and third-party scripts. Common culprits include analytics tools, A/B testing platforms like Kameleoon, Facebook tracking, PayPal iframes, and certain CMS configurations. Monitoring BFCache through CrUX, RUM tools, DevTools, and the Performance API helps identify eviction reasons. Working with third-party providers to fix blocking issues can significantly improve user experience at no implementation cost.

top_posts.title: The Old Ways Are the Best: 100 Lighthouse, 0ms TBT, 32ms Queries
top_posts.summary: A developer achieves exceptional performance metrics (100 Lighthouse score, 0ms Total Blocking Time, 32ms queries) by rejecting modern frameworks in favor of older techniques. The approach uses DATAOS (DOM As The Authority On State), treating the DOM itself as the state container instead of maintaining separate state objects, eliminating reconciliation overhead. On the backend, 1972-era bitmap indexing with RoaringBitmaps enables constant-time queries regardless of dataset size. The resulting application uses 32KB of vanilla JavaScript (15% of React's size) with a total payload under 100KB, demonstrating that native browser APIs and decades-old database techniques can outperform contemporary frameworks for most web applications.

top_posts.title: Web Performance Calendar
top_posts.summary: Fabian Krumbholz, a web performance consultant, highlights the importance of visualization tools for optimizing web performance. He focuses on two types of graphs: prioritization graphs, which help identify areas with the biggest impact, and timeseries graphs, which aid in understanding performance regressions. These graphs simplify complex data, enabling quicker decision-making and effective troubleshooting.
